title: A Comprehensive Review of Autophagy and Its Various Roles in Infectious, Non-Infectious, and Lifestyle Diseases: Current Knowledge and Prospects for Disease Prevention, Novel Drug Design, and Therapy

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts and Molecular Mechanisms of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Because autophagy is dynamic, its measurement must distinguish increased autophagosome formation from impaired clearance. Current best practice therefore emphasizes autophagic flux rather than static abundance of vesicles or markers ref [1]. Electron microscopy remains the ultrastructural benchmark for identifying double-membraned autophagosomes, but fixation artifacts and the difficulty of discriminating autophagosomes from related vacuolar structures limit stand-alone interpretation ref [1]. Accordingly, morphology is usually paired with biochemical or reporter-based assays.

In cultured cells, LC3-II immunoblotting with lysosomal inhibition and parallel assessment of SQSTM1/p62 remain the most widely used flux assays, provided results are interpreted against controls that block lysosomal degradation rather than as LC3-II snapshots alone ref [1]. Complementary approaches include quantification of LC3 puncta, long-lived protein degradation, and tandem fluorescent LC3 reporters such as mRFP-GFP-LC3, which exploit acid-sensitive GFP quenching to discriminate autophagosomes from autolysosomes ref [1]. Keima-based probes and GFP-LC3-RFP-LC3ΔG further improve quantitative tracking of lysosomal delivery, including selective cargo turnover such as mitophagy ref [1].

Flow cytometry has expanded throughput and single-cell resolution. Quantitative ratiometric analysis of mCherry-EGFP-LC3 enables direct stratification of basal and stimulus-induced flux in heterogeneous populations and even physical sorting of cells with high versus low autophagic flux for downstream functional studies ref [2]. This approach is especially valuable where cell-state heterogeneity obscures bulk measurements, although it still requires careful calibration of reporter expression, gating, and orthogonal validation ref [2]. In vivo, GFP-LC3, tandem fluorescent LC3, and mitophagy reporter mice are informative, but robust flux measurements in human tissues remain technically limited and vulnerable to overinterpretation from static specimens ref [1].

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts and Molecular Mechanisms of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Core Autophagy Pathway and Conceptual Framework
subsections.content:
Autophagy is a conserved lysosomal degradation pathway in which cytoplasmic material is sequestered within a double-membrane autophagosome and then delivered for breakdown and recycling, thereby coupling quality control with metabolic adaptation ref [3], ref [5]. Conceptually, the pathway is best viewed as an ordered flux rather than a static vesicle count: induction, phagophore nucleation, membrane expansion and closure, lysosomal fusion, cargo degradation, and metabolite efflux are mechanistically distinct but functionally integrated steps ref [3], ref [5].

The core machinery was defined genetically in yeast and is organized into modules that are largely conserved in mammals: the ULK/Atg1 kinase complex for early pathway engagement, the class III PI3K complex centered on VPS34–Beclin 1 for phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate generation, the ATG9 membrane-cycling system, and two ubiquitin-like conjugation cascades that generate the ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 complex and lipidated ATG8-family proteins such as LC3 and GABARAP ref [3], ref [5]. These modules coordinate autophagosome assembly while also providing nodes for regulation by nutrient, growth factor, and stress signaling ref [3], ref [5].

A key conceptual advance in mammalian systems is that autophagy operates as an interaction network rather than an isolated linear pathway. Proteomic mapping revealed extensive crosstalk among ULK, PI3KC3–BECN1, ATG8, trafficking, and kinase subnetworks, helping explain how basal and induced autophagy can support both bulk turnover and more selective cargo handling ref [4]. This framework also clarifies why autophagy is multifunctional in disease: defects can arise from impaired initiation, defective cargo capture, failed lysosomal clearance, or disrupted network connectivity, each producing distinct pathological outcomes despite sharing the label of 'autophagy deficiency' ref [3], ref [4], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts and Molecular Mechanisms of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagosome Biogenesis, Trafficking, and Lysosomal Delivery
subsections.content:
Autophagosome biogenesis proceeds through nucleation of a PI3P-enriched omegasome/phagophore, expansion of the isolation membrane, and sealing into a double-membrane vesicle. Current models emphasize the coordinated action of the ULK1 and class III PI3K complexes, WIPI proteins, the ATG12–ATG5–ATG16L1 conjugation system, and ATG8-family lipidation, while membrane input can derive from the ER, ERGIC, Golgi, plasma membrane, mitochondria, and recycling endosomes ref [6]. A particularly important element is ATG9, the only core transmembrane ATG protein, which cycles through Golgi- and endosome-related compartments and transiently contacts forming phagophores rather than becoming stably incorporated into autophagosomal membranes ref [6], ref [8].

Ultrastructural and live-cell analyses have refined this view by showing that ATG9 resides in specialized tubulovesicular reservoirs that contribute to the earliest membrane templates for PAS/phagophore formation in yeast, supporting a de novo assembly model for the nascent sequestering membrane ref [8]. In mammalian cells, ATG9 trafficking is regulated by ULK1- and Src-dependent phosphorylation and by recycling endosome dynamics, coupling membrane delivery with phagophore growth and closure ref [6]. After completion, autophagosomes undergo centripetal transport and mature through sequential fusion with endosomes and lysosomes, generating amphisomes and ultimately autolysosomes, where cargo is exposed to acidic hydrolases for degradation ref [6].

Lysosomal delivery is not merely a terminal fusion event but part of a broader maturation continuum. Evidence from Drosophila indicates that Atg9 also supports intraluminal vesicle formation and compartmentalized acidification within amphisomes and autolysosomes, linking ATG9 function to degradative competence as well as early biogenesis ref [7]. Thus, autophagosome formation, trafficking, and lysosomal fusion are best understood as an integrated membrane-remodeling pathway in which ATG9-positive compartments coordinate both the birth of the autophagosome and its productive maturation toward cargo destruction ref [6], ref [7], ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts and Molecular Mechanisms of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Selective Autophagy Modalities and Receptor Systems
subsections.content:
Selective autophagy confers cargo specificity to the core pathway by coupling substrates to the phagophore through dedicated receptors that recognize ATG8-family proteins via LC3-interacting region (LIR) motifs and, in many cases, ubiquitin on damaged cargo. This logic was first defined in yeast mitophagy, where the outer mitochondrial membrane receptor Atg32 engages Atg8 and the scaffold Atg11, establishing a paradigm for receptor-mediated organelle turnover ref [9], ref [10]. In mammals, analogous receptor systems extend this principle to mitochondria, protein aggregates, pathogens, lipid droplets, and peroxisomes, with SQSTM1/p62, NBR1, OPTN, NDP52/CALCOCO2, and TAX1BP1 acting as major ubiquitin-binding adaptors, while organelle-resident receptors can directly tether cargo to LC3/GABARAP proteins.

Mitophagy is the best-characterized selective modality. Developmental mitochondrial clearance in reticulocytes depends on NIX/BNIP3L, and related pathways employ BNIP3 and FUNDC1 as mitochondrial receptors whose LIR-dependent LC3 binding is regulated by stress or hypoxia ref [10], ref [11]. In parallel, PINK1-Parkin signaling marks damaged mitochondria with ubiquitin chains that recruit cytosolic receptors, integrating receptor-mediated and ubiquitin-dependent recognition into a unified quality-control framework ref [10]. Chaperone-mediated autophagy represents a mechanistically distinct selective pathway in which soluble proteins bearing KFERQ-like motifs are recognized by HSC70 and delivered individually across the lysosomal membrane via LAMP-2A, the CMA receptor originally identified by Cuervo and Dice ref [12], ref [13]. Dynamic assembly of LAMP-2A into translocation complexes further regulates substrate flux and selectivity at the lysosomal surface ref [14].

Conceptually, receptor systems determine not only what is degraded but also when and why autophagy is engaged in physiology and disease. Developmental organelle clearance, metabolic rewiring, mitochondrial quality control, and proteostasis all depend on the availability, post-translational regulation, and cargo affinity of these receptors ref [10], ref [11], ref [12]. This receptor-centric view is therefore central to understanding how dysregulated autophagy contributes to infectious, degenerative, metabolic, and lifestyle-associated disorders, and it provides an attractive basis for therapeutic strategies that aim to enhance or redirect cargo selectivity rather than globally activating autophagy.

subsections.section_title: Foundational Concepts and Molecular Mechanisms of Autophagy
subsections.subsection_title: Initiation and Signaling Control of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Autophagy initiation is organized around nutrient- and energy-sensing kinase networks that converge on the Atg1/ULK complex. In yeast, TORC1 directly phosphorylates Atg13, thereby preventing productive Atg1 complex activation under nutrient-rich conditions; starvation-driven TORC1 inhibition rapidly dephosphorylates Atg13 and permits Atg1-dependent autophagy induction [ref 1]. In mammals, the homologous ULK1/2-ATG13-FIP200 module is constitutive in composition rather than assembly, with FIP200 functioning as a key scaffold analogous in part to yeast Atg17 and being required for early autophagosome formation [ref 2]. mTORC1 associates with the ULK1 complex and suppresses ULK1 activity through inhibitory phosphorylation, whereas AMPK counteracts this repression during energetic stress, creating a central AMPK-mTOR-ULK signaling axis with multiple feedbacks and shortcuts [ref 7].

Upstream signaling is highly integrated. Growth factors and amino acids activate mTORC1, whereas glucose deprivation, hypoxia, and other stresses activate AMPK, which inhibits mTORC1 and can also directly stimulate ULK1/2 [ref 7]. Downstream of ULK, the class III PI3K nucleation machinery is engaged through Beclin 1-containing complexes, and Beclin 1 serves as a major phospho-regulated hub integrating pro-autophagic and inhibitory inputs from ULK1, AMPK, DAPK, Akt, EGFR, and other kinases [ref 5]. These phosphorylation events modulate Beclin 1 interactions with BCL2 family proteins, ATG14, UVRAG, and VPS34, thereby coupling autophagy initiation to stress adaptation, apoptosis crosstalk, and context-dependent cell fate decisions [ref 5].

Autophagy control also includes timed shutdown and organelle recovery. During prolonged starvation, lysosomal degradation products can reactivate mTOR, which attenuates further autophagy and drives autophagic lysosome reformation, restoring functional lysosomes from autolysosomal membranes [ref 3]. Thus, initiation and signaling control of autophagy should be viewed not as a simple on/off switch, but as a dynamic circuit in which TORC1, AMPK, ULK1/2-FIP200-ATG13, and Beclin 1-centered PI3K complexes coordinate induction, amplitude, and termination of the pathway across changing metabolic states [ref 1, ref 3, ref 7].

subsections.section_title: Physiological and Pathophysiological Roles of Autophagy in Infectious and Non-Infectious Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Immunity, Inflammation, and Host Homeostasis
subsections.content:
Autophagy is a core homeostatic pathway that links cellular quality control to immune surveillance, inflammatory restraint, and adaptation to stress. Beyond its canonical recycling role, autophagy intersects with innate and adaptive immunity at multiple levels, including pathogen sensing, cytokine regulation, lymphocyte homeostasis, and tissue protection, thereby acting as a rheostat that balances protective versus injurious host responses ref [20], ref [21], ref [23], ref [24], ref [25]. This integrative function helps explain why autophagy defects are increasingly associated not only with infection, but also with chronic inflammatory and autoimmune disorders ref [21], ref [24], ref [25].

Mechanistically, autophagy contributes to innate immunity by targeting intracellular danger signals and damaged organelles for lysosomal clearance, thereby limiting reactive oxygen species accumulation and inflammasome activation while preserving cellular fitness under stress ref [21], ref [24], ref [25]. Redox signaling is itself coupled to autophagic control: endogenous HMGB1 promotes autophagy through Beclin 1-dependent mechanisms and links oxidative stress to cytoprotective responses ref [26]. Selective autophagic turnover also interfaces with iron metabolism through ferritinophagy, which modulates intracellular iron availability, oxidative injury, and ferroptotic susceptibility, highlighting a broader role for autophagy in host metabolic homeostasis ref [27].

Autophagy also shapes adaptive immunity by supplying endogenous cytosolic antigens to MHC class II loading compartments, thereby expanding the antigenic repertoire available to CD4+ T cells and contributing to tolerance and immune education ref [22], ref [21], ref [24]. Early functional evidence that a cytosolic antigen can reach MHC class II via autophagy provided a key conceptual bridge between lysosomal self-digestion and antigen presentation ref [22]. In this context, autophagy is best viewed as a double-edged but indispensable pathway: insufficient flux favors inflammatory dysregulation and defective tolerance, whereas context-dependent activation sustains host homeostasis and immune competence ref [21], ref [23], ref [24], ref [25].

subsections.section_title: Physiological and Pathophysiological Roles of Autophagy in Infectious and Non-Infectious Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Antimicrobial Defense and Bacterial Pathogenesis
subsections.content:
Autophagy is a major arm of cell-autonomous antibacterial defense, but in bacterial infection it functions as both a degradative pathway and a contested intracellular niche. In xenophagy, damaged pathogen vacuoles or cytosolic bacteria are marked by ubiquitin and sensed by receptors such as p62, NDP52, and OPTN, which couple microbes to LC3-positive membranes for lysosomal clearance ref [28], ref [29]. Salmonella provided a foundational model for this process: bacteria exposed by damaged Salmonella-containing vacuoles are rapidly decorated with ubiquitin and LC3, restricting intracellular replication ref [29].

Bacterial pathogens have therefore evolved highly specific countermeasures. Listeria monocytogenes evades recognition through ActA-mediated camouflage with host actin-polymerization machinery, thereby limiting ubiquitination and p62 recruitment, while additional virulence factors further suppress LC3 lipidation and pre-autophagosomal maturation ref [30]. Shigella flexneri similarly antagonizes autophagy through IcsB- and VirA-dependent mechanisms that block Atg5 recognition, Rab1 activity, LC3 recruitment, and septin cage formation, illustrating how distinct pathogens target different nodes of the pathway ref [31]. Broader surveys show that Salmonella, Legionella, Mycobacterium, and Group A Streptococcus also exploit deubiquitinases, autophagosome maturation defects, or receptor degradation to escape xenophagic killing ref [28], ref [7].

Importantly, autophagy can also be subverted to nourish intracellular bacteria. Reviews of pathogen metabolism emphasize that autophagic proteolysis increases pools of amino acids, lipids, and other metabolites that can be harvested for replication ref [32], ref [7]. Anaplasma phagocytophilum redirects its vacuole toward an early autophagosome-like compartment enriched in LC3 and Beclin 1, and pharmacologic induction of autophagy enhances bacterial growth ref [33]. Likewise, Salmonella can co-opt host chaperone-mediated autophagy to access host-derived peptides within the vacuole, underscoring that bacterial pathogenesis often depends not only on avoiding autophagic destruction but also on rewiring autophagy for nutrient acquisition and persistence ref [8].

subsections.section_title: Physiological and Pathophysiological Roles of Autophagy in Infectious and Non-Infectious Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Cancer: Tumor Suppression, Tumor Maintenance, and Therapy Response
subsections.content:
Autophagy exerts a stage-dependent and context-dependent role in cancer. In early tumorigenesis, basal autophagy limits oxidative stress, damaged organelle accumulation, and genome instability, thereby functioning as a barrier to malignant transformation. This tumor-suppressive role is strongly supported by Beclin 1 haploinsufficiency studies, in which monoallelic loss increased spontaneous malignancies without loss of the remaining allele, establishing autophagy deficiency as a driver rather than a bystander of oncogenesis ref [35], ref [37]. Complementary evidence from Atg5- and Atg7-deficient mouse models showed spontaneous liver adenomas and multiple liver tumors associated with p62 accumulation, oxidative stress, and DNA-damage responses ref [36]. Mechanistically, defective autophagy promotes chromosomal instability and gene amplification, linking impaired quality control to tumor progression ref [40].

In established cancers, however, autophagy often becomes a metabolic liability for the host but an adaptive advantage for the tumor. Ras-driven cancers are a paradigmatic example: oncogenic Ras elevates basal autophagy and requires it to sustain mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, survival during nutrient stress, and tumorigenesis ref [16]. More broadly, autophagy supports survival in hypoxic and therapy-stressed tumor regions, yet this same pathway can also intersect with senescence and dormancy programs that shape residual disease persistence and later relapse ref [18]. Thus, autophagy can both suppress tumor initiation and maintain advanced tumors, depending on genetic context, nutrient state, and disease stage ref [34].

These dual functions directly inform therapy. Pharmacologic autophagy inhibition, most commonly with chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine, can sensitize selected tumors to chemotherapy and radiotherapy, as shown in colorectal cancer models where chloroquine enhanced response to concurrent chemoradiation ref [13]. Conversely, indiscriminate autophagy blockade may remove a genome-protective barrier in premalignant tissues or favor inflammatory and metabolic adaptation in some settings ref [34], ref [40]. Current therapeutic strategies therefore increasingly emphasize context-specific autophagy modulation, biomarker-guided patient selection, and rational combination regimens rather than uniform inhibition or activation.

subsections.section_title: Physiological and Pathophysiological Roles of Autophagy in Infectious and Non-Infectious Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Viral Infection: Antiviral Restriction Versus Proviral Subversion of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Autophagy exerts bona fide antiviral activity by promoting virophagy, innate sensing, and antigen presentation, but viruses frequently evolve countermeasures to block these restrictive outputs. A seminal in vivo study showed that Beclin 1 protects against lethal Sindbis virus encephalitis, establishing autophagy as a host defense mechanism in viral infection ref [42]. More broadly, autophagy can deliver viral nucleic acids to endosomal sensors and facilitate MHC presentation, whereas several viral factors directly antagonize Beclin 1-dependent autophagy, illustrating a recurrent host–virus arms race ref [44], ref [43], ref [9].

Conversely, many RNA viruses co-opt autophagy or autophagy-like membranes as replication platforms while preventing their lysosomal destruction. Coxsackievirus B3 induces double-membrane vesicles, increases LC3 lipidation, and requires Beclin 1, VPS34, and ATG7 for efficient replication, with blockade of autophagosome maturation further enhancing viral yield ref [47]. Hepatitis C virus likewise triggers an unfolded protein response–dependent but incomplete autophagic program that supports viral RNA replication rather than cargo degradation ref [49], ref [45]. Influenza A virus also benefits from autophagy, as pharmacologic or genetic inhibition of LC3/Beclin 1 reduces viral protein accumulation and progeny production ref [11].

HIV exemplifies the duality of this pathway. Acute HIV-1 infection suppresses Beclin 1 expression, LC3-II accumulation, and autophagosome abundance in CD4+ T cells and monocytic cells ref [14]. Yet in macrophages, basal autophagy promotes Gag processing and viral yield, while Nef binds Beclin 1 to inhibit autophagosome maturation and thereby protect viral components from autolysosomal degradation ref [15]. In coronaviruses, autophagy induction and LC3 redistribution are commonly observed, but dependence on canonical ATG5-mediated autophagy is context dependent; some studies instead implicate noncanonical LC3-associated membranes or ER-derived vesicles in replication complex biogenesis ref [20], ref [46], ref [10]. Thus, in viral infection, autophagy is best viewed not as uniformly protective or pathogenic, but as a contested pathway whose outcome depends on the balance between antiviral restriction and proviral subversion ref [44].

subsections.section_title: Physiological and Pathophysiological Roles of Autophagy in Infectious and Non-Infectious Diseases
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy in Neurodegenerative, Cardiac, and Metabolic Diseases
subsections.content:
Autophagy is a major homeostatic pathway in postmitotic tissues, and its dysfunction is strongly implicated in neurodegeneration. In Alzheimer disease, beclin 1 is reduced early in affected brain regions, and experimental beclin 1 deficiency aggravates amyloid-β accumulation and neurodegeneration, whereas beclin 1 restoration mitigates pathology ref [57]. In Parkinson disease, wild-type α-synuclein can be cleared by both chaperone-mediated autophagy and macroautophagy, while autophagy enhancement with trehalose or beclin 1 gene transfer accelerates clearance of toxic α-synuclein species and improves synaptic-neuritic phenotypes in model systems ref [9], ref [11], ref [13]. Likewise, autophagy genes protect against toxicity from polyglutamine-expanded proteins, supporting a broader role in limiting aggregate proteotoxicity across Huntington-like disorders ref [18].

A related axis of disease control is mitophagy. PINK1 accumulation on damaged mitochondria recruits and activates Parkin, initiating selective mitochondrial turnover ref [17]. This pathway has become central to Parkinson disease biology, although in vivo evidence indicates that its physiological contribution is context-dependent and incompletely resolved, with important differences between toxin-based cell systems and intact organisms ref [15]. Nonetheless, defective mitochondrial quality control is increasingly viewed as a mechanism linking impaired autophagy to neuronal vulnerability, oxidative stress, and progressive degeneration ref [15], ref [17].

Outside the nervous system, autophagy exerts similarly nuanced effects in cardiac and metabolic disease. In load-induced heart disease, basal autophagy appears necessary for proteostasis, whereas excessive stress-induced autophagy can become maladaptive and contribute to adverse remodeling and heart failure progression ref [20]. In metabolic tissues, autophagy and especially chaperone-mediated autophagy regulate lipid handling, glucose homeostasis, and organelle quality control; disruption of these processes promotes insulin resistance, steatosis, and broader metabolic dysfunction ref [21], ref [22]. Collectively, these findings position autophagy as a context-dependent determinant of tissue resilience and a promising, but carefully titrated, therapeutic target across neurodegenerative, cardiac, and metabolic disorders ref [11], ref [13], ref [20], ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy: Inhibitors, Activators, and Clinical Strategies
subsections.content:
mTOR is a central negative regulator of macroautophagy, integrating nutrient and growth-factor signals to suppress ULK1-dependent autophagosome biogenesis; accordingly, pharmacologic mTOR inhibition by rapamycin and its derivatives remains the canonical strategy for mTOR-dependent autophagy activation. Rapalogs such as temsirolimus/CCI-779 and everolimus were initially advanced in oncology because they inhibit mTOR signaling, reduce phosphorylation of downstream effectors including p70S6K and 4E-BP1, and show manageable if mechanism-linked toxicities, notably mucositis, rash, metabolic disturbances, and dose-dependent cytopenias ref [59].

Beyond cancer, rapalog-induced autophagy has shown disease-modifying potential in proteinopathy models. In mutant tau transgenic mice, the rapamycin ester analog CCI-779/temsirolimus crossed into the CNS sufficiently to suppress mTOR signaling, increase LC3-II and Rab7, reduce Sarkosyl-insoluble tau and phospho-tau, lower neurofibrillary tangle burden, and improve motor performance when treatment was initiated before overt deficits ref [58]. Related work with rapamycin in tauopathy and Alzheimer-like models similarly indicated that early mTOR inhibition is more effective than late intervention, emphasizing a narrow therapeutic window for autophagy-based proteostasis rescue. In parallel, rapamycin enhanced repressed autophagy in experimental IgA nephropathy, reduced p-mTOR/p-S6K1 and cyclin D1, and attenuated proteinuria, mesangial proliferation, and renal injury, linking mTOR-dependent autophagy restoration to renoprotection ref [61].

A key limitation of first-generation rapalogs is that antitumor and pro-autophagic benefit may be offset by incomplete mTOR inhibition, feedback signaling, and immunosuppressive liability. This has motivated adjunctive strategies that potentiate rapamycin responses. Small-molecule enhancers of rapamycin (SMERs) were identified through chemical-genetic screening and were shown to augment rapamycin-associated TOR inhibition, promote autophagy, reduce mutant huntingtin toxicity, and enhance mycobacterial killing by macrophages, thereby illustrating how combination approaches can widen the therapeutic index of mTOR-directed autophagy activation ref [5]. Collectively, rapalogs established the clinical proof-of-principle that mTOR inhibition can mobilize autophagy in vivo, but their future utility will likely depend on disease timing, tissue penetration, biomarker-guided dosing, and rational combinations that preserve autophagic efficacy while minimizing systemic toxicity ref [58], ref [59], ref [61], ref [5].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy: Inhibitors, Activators, and Clinical Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: MicroRNA and Acetylation-Based Therapeutic Regulation of Autophagy
subsections.content:
Beyond kinase-centered control, autophagy is also therapeutically tunable through post-transcriptional and epigenetic circuits. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate virtually every stage of the pathway, targeting initiators such as ULK1/2, nucleation components including BECN1 and ATG14, elongation factors such as ATG5, ATG7, ATG16L1 and LC3, and upstream mTOR regulators ref [5]. Representative examples include miR-30a-mediated repression of BECN1, miR-101 targeting of RAB5A and ATG4 family members, miR-375 suppression of ATG7, miR-23b inhibition of ATG12, and miR-155 or miR-100 activation of autophagy through mTOR-pathway inhibition ref [5]. Notably, autophagy also feeds back on miRNA homeostasis by promoting turnover of DICER, AGO2, AIN-1/GW182, or even mature miRNAs in selected settings, indicating a bidirectional regulatory loop ref [5].

This network has clear therapeutic implications. In cancer models, autophagy-suppressive miRNAs such as miR-30a, miR-101, miR-199a-5p, miR-205, and miR-23b can sensitize tumor cells to imatinib, cisplatin, tamoxifen, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy by disabling cytoprotective autophagy, whereas in other contexts restoration of pro-autophagic miRNAs may enhance stress-induced tumor cell death ref [5]. More broadly, miRNA control of IRGM- and ATG16L1-dependent pathways links autophagy modulation to host defense and inflammatory disease, including Crohn's disease and epithelial antibacterial responses ref [5]. Translation remains constrained by delivery, durability, and off-target effects, but antagomirs, locked-nucleic-acid inhibitors, viral vectors, lipid nanoparticles, and polymeric nanocarriers have all shown preclinical feasibility for rewiring autophagy through miRNA circuits ref [5].

Acetylation provides a complementary pharmacologic lever. The acetyltransferase p300 acetylates core autophagy proteins including ATG5, ATG7, LC3/ATG8, and ATG12, physically associates with ATG7, and suppresses autophagic flux; conversely, p300 knockdown reduces ATG acetylation, increases LC3-II formation and GFP-LC3 puncta, lowers p62, and thereby stimulates autophagy ref [6]. Nutrient deprivation weakens the p300-ATG7 interaction, supporting a model in which starvation-induced deacetylation favors autophagy ref [6]. Together with prior evidence for SIRT1-dependent deacetylation, these findings position the p300/SIRT1 axis as a druggable rheostat for autophagy, with potential relevance to cancer, degeneration, metabolic stress, and combination therapy strategies in which miRNA- and acetylation-based interventions are paired with canonical autophagy modulators ref [5], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy: Inhibitors, Activators, and Clinical Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Autophagy Modulation in Host Defense, Degeneration, and Clinical Translation
subsections.content:
Autophagy modulation in host defense has advanced from descriptive biology to actionable host-directed therapy. In tuberculosis, phenotypic screening of infected macrophages identified clinically used compounds such as fluoxetine and the EGFR inhibitor gefitinib that restrict intracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis by enhancing autophagy and, in the case of fluoxetine, pro-inflammatory TNF-α signaling; importantly, gefitinib also reduced pulmonary mycobacterial burden in mice, illustrating translational potential for repurposed autophagy-modulating drugs ref [64]. A complementary screen revealed anticonvulsants, especially carbamazepine and valproic acid, as enhancers of mTOR-independent autophagic killing through inositol depletion, with carbamazepine improving clearance in zebrafish and reducing burden and pathology in a multidrug-resistant tuberculosis mouse model ref [65]. Together, these studies support autophagy activation as a host-targeted strategy that may complement conventional antimicrobials, particularly where pathogen drug resistance limits direct antibacterial options ref [64], ref [65].

The same principle extends beyond mycobacterial infection to epithelial barrier defense. In Caenorhabditis elegans, bacterial pore-forming toxins activate HLH-30/TFEB-dependent autophagy in intestinal cells, where the response acts cell-autonomously to promote xenophagic toxin clearance and membrane-pore repair, thereby increasing organismal tolerance to intoxication ref [7]. This work is conceptually important for clinical translation because it links TFEB-like transcriptional control, selective degradation of damaging microbial effectors, and epithelial resilience in a whole-animal setting ref [7]. More broadly, these findings reinforce that therapeutic benefit may derive not only from suppressing pathogen replication, but also from strengthening tissue-intrinsic damage control pathways.

In degenerative settings, the translational logic is analogous: pharmacologic enhancement of autophagic flux can facilitate removal of toxic protein species and damaged organelles, but clinical deployment requires matching mechanism to disease context and avoiding maladaptive overactivation. The infection literature now provides a practical template for this transition, emphasizing repurposed agents, in vivo validation, and biomarker-linked patient stratification ref [64], ref [65], ref [7]. Thus, current clinical translation increasingly views autophagy not as a single on/off process, but as a tunable host-protective network whose therapeutic value depends on cell type, disease stage, and the balance between microbial control, stress adaptation, and tissue preservation.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy: Inhibitors, Activators, and Clinical Strategies
subsections.subsection_title: Pharmacologic Autophagy Inhibitors and Lysosomal Blockade
subsections.content:
Pharmacologic inhibition of autophagy is dominated by agents that block late-stage flux at the lysosome, most notably chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine, bafilomycin A1, and newer dimeric quinolines such as Lys05. Mechanistically, these compounds impair autophagosome clearance by disrupting lysosomal acidification, degradative capacity, or autophagosome–lysosome fusion, thereby causing LC3-II and often SQSTM1/p62 accumulation rather than productive catabolism ref [67], ref [68], ref [69], ref [70]. Bafilomycin A1, a vacuolar H+-ATPase inhibitor, remains a canonical experimental tool for lysosomal blockade, although its effects can extend beyond simple flux arrest and may engage apoptosis-related programs in some malignancies ref [67]. Genetic disruption of the v-ATPase machinery likewise produces marked accumulation of autophagic vacuoles and lysosomes, underscoring that lysosomal failure can uncouple vacuole buildup from straightforward MTORC1 suppression ref [68].

The translational limitation of first-generation lysosomotropic agents has driven efforts to develop more potent compounds. Lys05, a bisaminoquinoline derivative, accumulates within lysosomes more efficiently than hydroxychloroquine, produces stronger deacidification and autophagic vacuole accumulation, and shows single-agent antitumor activity while recapitulating features of genetic autophagy deficiency in vivo ref [69]. These observations support the concept that deeper lysosomal blockade can expose autophagy dependence in tumors, but they also highlight the narrow therapeutic window of systemic autophagy inhibition. Consistent with this caution, bafilomycin A1 has shown selective antileukemic activity in pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, where low-dose treatment inhibited cytoprotective autophagy while also activating apoptosis pathways ref [67].

A major caveat is that lysosomal autophagy inhibitors can perturb mitochondrial homeostasis and cellular metabolism independently of disease-specific mechanisms. In primary neurons, both bafilomycin A1 and chloroquine reduced basal and maximal respiration, impaired respiratory complex-linked bioenergetics, increased mitochondrial DNA damage, and altered tricarboxylic acid cycle intermediates, consistent with defective mitochondrial quality control after autophagy blockade ref [70]. Accordingly, clinical deployment of lysosomal inhibitors should be interpreted as modulation of the autophagy–lysosome system broadly, not merely as selective suppression of autophagosome turnover, and will likely require context-specific biomarkers of flux, lysosomal function, and tissue toxicity.

subsections.section_title: Therapeutic Modulation of Autophagy: Inhibitors, Activators, and Clinical Strategies
subsections.content:
mTOR-independent autophagy activation has attracted sustained interest because it may avoid the pleiotropic liabilities of chronic mTOR suppression while still promoting cargo clearance. A central paradigm is inositol/IP3 signaling: lithium induces autophagy by inhibiting inositol monophosphatase (IMPase), lowering free inositol and IP3, and thereby enhancing the clearance of mutant huntingtin and A53T/A30P α-synuclein through a mechanism separable from mTOR inhibition ref [6], ref [8]. This concept was extended by broader surveys of autophagy-inducing chemicals showing that carbamazepine and valproate share related inositol-lowering effects and can cooperate conceptually with mTOR-targeted approaches in proteotoxic disease models ref [10].

Trehalose represents another prototypical mTOR-independent activator. Initially characterized as a disaccharide that accelerates clearance of mutant huntingtin and α-synuclein, trehalose later proved mechanistically more tractable when it was shown to inhibit SLC2A/GLUT-mediated glucose transport, generating a starvation-like state that activates AMPK and ULK1 and stimulates autophagic flux ref [71], ref [10]. This mechanism helps explain trehalose activity across models of Huntington’s disease, ALS, tauopathy, and hepatic steatosis, and also illustrates that “mTOR-independent” activation can still converge on canonical initiation machinery downstream of cellular energy stress ref [71].

Chemical screening has further broadened the mTOR-independent repertoire to include SMERs, L-type Ca2+ channel blockers, calpain inhibitors, imidazoline receptor agonists, adenylyl cyclase/Gs inhibitors, and other agents that converge on a Ca2+-calpain-cAMP-IP3 regulatory circuit ref [10]. These compounds enhance autophagic flux and reduce aggregate burden in cellular and in vivo neurodegeneration models, while combinations with rapamycin may yield additive effects by engaging parallel pathways ref [8], ref [10]. Nevertheless, translation remains constrained by context dependence, dose sensitivity, and the need to distinguish true flux induction from impaired lysosomal turnover, particularly for agents such as lithium whose effects can vary across disease states ref [6], ref [10].
